title: States of matter, phase changes and gas laws
blurb: Describe solids, liquids and gases, name every phase change with its energy direction, read a heating curve and apply the basic gas laws.
question: A beaker of ice at −20 °C is heated steadily until it is all steam. Why does the thermometer stop rising twice along the way, and which of the changes absorb heat?

teach.body: Formally, the kinetic molecular theory says matter is made of particles in constant motion, and temperature measures their average kinetic energy. In plain English: the hotter something is, the faster its particles move on average. How tightly the particles are held decides the state. Heat is energy that flows because of a temperature difference, by conduction, convection or radiation.

teach.caption: Plasma, the fourth state, is an ionized gas with no fixed shape or volume: stars, lightning, neon signs.

head: Change
From → to
Heat
teach.caption: Toward gas absorbs heat; toward solid releases it. Dry ice, iodine and mothballs sublime; frost forms by deposition.
Flat plateau at 0 °C: melting (heat of fusion). Longer plateau at 100 °C: boiling (heat of vaporization). The slopes are single-phase warming.

teach.h: Plateaus: temperature holds during a phase change
teach.body: While a substance melts or boils, the added energy goes into breaking the attractions between particles, not into speeding them up, so the temperature stays constant until the change is complete. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point; evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature. Evaporation absorbs heat, which is why sweat cools the body.

Gas particles are far apart, so a gas's pressure, volume and temperature are linked. Boyle's law: at constant temperature, squeezing a gas into a smaller volume raises its pressure (inverse; this is how breathing works). Charles's law: at constant pressure, heating a gas makes it expand (direct, using kelvin). Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, heating raises pressure. All combine in PV = nRT. STP is 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm.

head: Law
Held constant
Relationship
Example
teach.caption: Temperatures in gas-law calculations must be in kelvin: K = °C + 273.

teach.body: Malik, a phlebotomy student, seals the tip of a syringe holding 10 mL of air at 1 atm and pushes the plunger until the volume is 5 mL. Temperature is unchanged, so Boyle's law applies: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so 1 × 10 = P₂ × 5, giving P₂ = 2 atm. Halving the volume doubled the pressure: an inverse relationship.

teach.text: Sublimation is solid → gas; deposition is gas → solid. Condensation and freezing RELEASE heat; melting and boiling ABSORB it. Temperature does not rise during melting. Liquids DO have a definite volume (just not a definite shape). And never use Celsius in Charles's law: convert to kelvin first.

items: Solid: definite shape and volume. Liquid: definite volume only. Gas: neither, and compressible.
Temperature = average kinetic energy of the particles.
Melting, vaporization, sublimation absorb heat; freezing, condensation, deposition release it.
Temperature is constant during a phase change; water melts at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at 1 atm.
Boyle: P up, V down. Charles: T up, V up (kelvin). Gay-Lussac: T up, P up.

summary: You can now compare solids, liquids and gases, name all six phase changes with their energy direction and explain the flat plateaus on a heating curve. You can also apply Boyle's, Charles's and Gay-Lussac's laws, converting to kelvin when temperature is involved.

A.q: Which state of matter has a definite volume but takes the shape of its container?
A.why: Liquid particles are close together (fixed volume) but slide past one another, so a liquid takes its container's shape.

whyNot.1: A solid keeps both its own shape and its volume.
whyNot.2: A gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume; it fills its container.
whyNot.3: Plasma is an ionized gas with no fixed shape or volume.

A.q: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) turns directly into gas at room temperature. What is this phase change called?
A.why: Sublimation is the change from solid straight to gas, skipping the liquid state.

whyNot.0: Evaporation is liquid to gas at a liquid's surface.
whyNot.1: Deposition is the reverse: gas straight to solid, as when frost forms.

A.q: Which phase change releases heat to the surroundings?
A.why: Condensation (gas to liquid) is exothermic: particles come together and release energy.

whyNot.0: Melting absorbs heat to separate particles in the solid.
whyNot.1: Sublimation absorbs heat to turn a solid directly into a gas.
whyNot.2: Vaporization absorbs heat (the heat of vaporization).

B.q: What does the temperature of a substance measure?
options: The total heat energy held by a sample
The potential energy stored in bonds
B.why: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles.

whyNot.0: Total thermal energy depends on the amount of substance; temperature is an average.
whyNot.2: Bond (potential) energy changes during phase changes while temperature stays constant.
whyNot.3: Collisions increase with temperature, but temperature measures average kinetic energy.

B.q: Ice at 0 °C is heated steadily on a hot plate. While the ice is melting, the thermometer reading:
options: climbs steadily as the ice melts
falls slightly as the ice melts
climbs once half the ice has melted
holds at 0 °C until it has melted
B.why: During a phase change the energy breaks attractions between particles, so temperature stays at the melting point until all the ice has melted.

whyNot.0: A steady climb happens only after melting is complete, when the liquid warms.
whyNot.1: Heat is being added, so the temperature does not fall.
whyNot.2: The temperature stays flat for the whole plateau, not just the first half.

B.q: At the top of a high mountain, water boils below 100 °C. Why?
options: There is less oxygen in the air
B.why: Boiling point depends on the surrounding pressure; lower air pressure at altitude lowers the boiling point.

whyNot.1: Air temperature affects how fast water heats, not the temperature at which it boils.
whyNot.2: Water's heat capacity does not change with altitude; pressure is what changes.
whyNot.3: Oxygen content does not set the boiling point; total air pressure does.

C.q: A 6 L sample of gas at 1 atm is compressed at constant temperature until its pressure is 3 atm. What is its new volume?
C.why: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so 1 × 6 = 3 × V₂ and V₂ = 2 L. Tripling the pressure cuts the volume to one-third.

whyNot.0: 18 L treats pressure and volume as directly proportional; Boyle's law is inverse.
whyNot.1: 3 L halves the volume (6 ÷ 2), but tripling the pressure cuts the volume to one-third, not one-half.
whyNot.3: 0.5 L inverts the ratio (3 ÷ 6); the volume is 6 × (1 ÷ 3).

C.q: A sealed balloon at constant pressure is warmed from 27 °C to 54 °C. What happens to its volume?
options: It doubles, to twice the original
It stays at its starting size
C.why: Charles's law needs kelvin: 300 K → 327 K. V₂/V₁ = 327/300 ≈ 1.09, so the volume rises by roughly 9%, about one-tenth.

whyNot.0: Doubling assumes the Celsius values can be used directly; in kelvin the temperature rose only from 300 to 327.
whyNot.2: Heating a gas at constant pressure makes it expand, not shrink.
whyNot.3: Volume and kelvin temperature are directly proportional, so warming changes the volume.

C.q: Which statement about phase changes is correct?
options: Freezing absorbs heat from the surroundings
Deposition turns a solid directly into a gas
Evaporation requires the liquid to be boiling
Evaporating sweat absorbs heat from skin
C.why: Vaporization (including evaporation) is endothermic, so evaporating sweat absorbs heat from the skin and cools the body.

whyNot.1: Solid to gas is sublimation; deposition is gas to solid.
whyNot.2: Evaporation occurs at a liquid's surface at any temperature; boiling happens at the boiling point.

reteach.title: A school's three settings
reteach.question: Think about students in an exam hall, on a crowded dance floor and at recess on an open field. How do these match solids, liquids and gases?

blocks.body: In the exam hall, students sit in fixed seats and only fidget: a solid. On the dance floor they are still close but move past each other: a liquid, keeping its crowd size but filling the room's shape. At recess they run in every direction and spread over the whole field: a gas. Energy moves them from one setting to the next. While they file out of the hall, their energy goes into leaving their seats, not running faster: that is why temperature pauses during a phase change.

blocks.text: Run the flow backward (freezing, condensing) and the energy is released, not absorbed.

explain.body: Solids: fixed shape and volume, particles vibrate in place. Liquids: fixed volume, take the container's shape. Gases: fill the container and are compressible. Plasma: ionized gas.

test.q: Which description fits the particles in a gas?
options: Far apart, moving fast and randomly
Close together, sliding past each other
Far apart, vibrating in fixed positions
test.why: Gas particles are widely spaced and move rapidly in random directions, which is why gases fill containers and compress.

whyNot.1: Close particles sliding past one another describe a liquid.
whyNot.2: Tightly packed particles vibrating in place describe a solid.
whyNot.3: Gas particles are not held in fixed positions; they move freely.

explain.body: Toward the gas state (melting, vaporization, sublimation) absorbs heat. Toward the solid state (condensation, freezing, deposition) releases heat.

test.q: Frost forms on a car windshield on a cold night as water vapor turns straight into ice. Which phase change is this?
test.why: Gas changing directly to solid is deposition.

whyNot.0: Sublimation is the reverse: solid directly to gas.
whyNot.1: Condensation is gas to liquid; frost skips the liquid stage.
whyNot.3: Freezing is liquid to solid; here the starting state is a gas.

explain.body: Sloped sections: one state warming up. Flat plateaus: a phase change, with energy breaking attractions so temperature holds. Water's plateaus sit at 0 °C and 100 °C at 1 atm.

test.q: On a heating curve, what do the flat sections represent?
options: Heat being lost to the surrounding air
A change of state at constant temperature
The particles' kinetic energy rising fastest
A chemical reaction absorbing the heat
test.why: The plateaus are phase changes: added energy breaks particle attractions, so temperature (average kinetic energy) stays constant.

whyNot.0: Heat is still being added during the plateaus; it is being used to change state.
whyNot.2: Kinetic energy, and so temperature, is constant on a plateau; it rises on the slopes.
whyNot.3: Melting and boiling are physical changes, not chemical reactions.

explain.body: Boyle (constant T): pressure and volume are inverse. Charles (constant P): volume and kelvin temperature are direct. Gay-Lussac (constant V): pressure and kelvin temperature are direct.

test.q: According to Charles's law, at constant pressure the volume of a gas:
options: halves if its kelvin temperature doubles
doubles if its Celsius temperature doubles
halves if the pressure on it is halved
doubles if its kelvin temperature doubles
test.why: Charles's law: V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ with T in kelvin, so volume is directly proportional to kelvin temperature.

whyNot.0: That describes an inverse relationship; Charles's law is direct.
whyNot.1: Celsius cannot be used; only kelvin temperature is proportional to volume.
whyNot.2: Pressure is held constant in Charles's law; halving pressure would actually double the volume (Boyle).
